title: How a film communicates / Values of Film

commenti.body:
If such things are of value to you, that's fine.

To me this is pointless.  I do not watch movies to pigeonhole them, to classify them, to analyze them; I do not use a movie as a data point to prove some theory about it is of value.  (To me, movies are not equations or puzzles, nor are they data.)  I watch them to enjoy them.

Some philosophers--e.g. Plato, Aristotle, Baumgartner, Kant, Schopenhauer, Tolstoy, Croce, Santanayana, and so on--have attempted to create aesthetic systems.  All they do is offer their own parochial and tendentious opinions about what they think aesthetics should be.

>people in stories must follow the social norms

and

>like what genre conventions it is expected to follow

I accept what a movie offers me, whether it attempts or does not attempt to follow some convention.  (And whether or not I am aware it attempts or does not attempt to do so.  I do not see it as my task when I watch a movie to create or refer to some encyclopedia of conventions--cliches, tropes.)  I consider expecting a movie to do anything is a mistake.  It implies that if a movie does not follow some convention, then it fails.  That penalizes a movie's uniqueness for no reason I can see.

I also think it gets the cause and effect wrong.  Here's an analogy.  (I know it fails in several ways but I think succeeds where it counts--it is an analogy, a metaphor, not a proof.)  Almost weekly I hear some on screen TV personality claim "The stock underperformed" or "Economists were expecting a lower inflation number."  Well, a stock price or economic indicator is a fact, a measurement, a datum arising from reality; expectation is typically an opinion arising solely from that analyst (his worldview, his models).  When a stock price and an analyst's expectation differ, it is the expectation which is wrong.  The difference is evidence the analyst does not understand what he is talking about.  (That may be because economics is complex, too complex for the analyst to understand.  Fine--yet they do not admit that, do they?  No, they imply they *do* understand, even as their expectations are often wrong.  It's funny.)  That is the opposite of science.  Scientists make predictions about phenomena.  (Consider Kepler and the Mars orbit.)  If a scientific prediction does not agree with reality, the prediction--the idea about reality--is wrong.  Reality is not wrong.   Ideas about reality may be wrong.  Yet the on screen TV personality typically implies it is the stock or indicator which is wrong, that reality is somehow wrong,  that the expectation is somehow right--even when it is wrong, and that somehow the rational thing to do is to punish the stock (with sell orders) or the administration in power (with lower approval ratings).

With movies, there is no right or wrong.  It is taste, the eye of the beholder.  Yet with that small difference, you are merely offering an aesthetic version of what economists do.  You imply your taste is right (right for you, right for humanity), even if it differs from mine.  (You do not speak for me.  I do not watch movies for the reason you do.)  How do you not see this?

A consensus is a collective opinion.  A collective opinion does not become a fact.  (An opinion, of one person or a billion, is not a truth.)  If everyone who had ever lived thought Plan 9 from Outer Space was the most enjoyable movie, I would not agree.  If everyone on Earth agreed that Chinese women should have small feet (and that parents should bind their feet, as related by Pearl Buck), I would not agree.  If everyone agreed people should wear a 17th century lace collar, I would not agree.  If everyone agreed people should buy a tulip even if it cost as much as a house, I would not agree.

A consensus about beauty or value can change in time and place.  It is not an invariant, and neither are conventions in movies.  A convention is not a truth.

>I think we (people who analyze films)

Obviously, you are not writing to me.  So you can ignore all of the above.

I don’t have time to go fully in depth on every question here, but the philosophy of art is something I think about very much. This isn’t really planned-out, so I don’t know how well I’m describing some of the ideas I have…

  
I think the greatest art comes from its creator expressing the most genuine feelings from their "soul".  It’s especially true of film, where a master can create a shot they don’t necessarily know the “meaning” of, but comes from the core of their being (While also being paired with the precision of narrative storytelling which can deliver a more concrete message). And because it comes from the core of their being, their soul, if you will, it also reflects what’s in any other person’s “Soul” I am a more religiously inclined and spiritual person, so I might see it differently than others, but I personally think there is an underlying unitary reality for all humans, sort of like the Brahman and Atman concept in Vedanta philosophy. But if you’re less religious, you could think of it as something like the concept of the collective unconscious.  
But since we’re all humans experiencing the same things, any person fully expressing their self innately connects to all humans.

  
But I also think that *uniqueness* is something that should be valued in film and art in general. I see it as an expression of the individual person’s self, while it still contains the same substance deeper down that all other great pieces of art do. Something that tries to be unique just for the sake of being unique might not be true to the human experience, and fall flat. 

Although I do agree that all art is subjective, because it's value comes from the mind, I do think there are ways of measuring the quality of a piece of art, since generally the mind works in patterns. Generally, the people who I've seen trying to shut down any criticism of film with "subjectivity", don't seem to be very well educated in these subjects at all, because it's like they're denying the fact that there are established techniques, canons, etc. entire schools dedicated to these thoughts, because some methods obviously do resonate with humans more than others. So there are *bad* films, yes, and I'd consider the creator not truly *feeling* or understanding what they are creating as the main factor. Not all good or great art has to have a deep philosophical meaning, but I think it will work as long as the creator has an understanding of what the things they are creating represent, to their own selves and to humanity as a whole.  
  
If you want to talk about how general societal norms are presented in films, that’s another interesting topic. If you’ve seen enough movies from different cultures, you will eventually realize the innate cultural norms and values that differ slightly in different places. But this also demonstrates that collective unconscious which art springs from, because while “Norms”, “Values”, etc. may differ among cultures, they are all expressions of morality, and no matter how much they may differ you will eventually see ethical systems are based on many of the same underlying principles, treating another as one would treat themselves, kindness, love. Whether you want to say they are deeper spiritual concepts, or just mechanisms we’ve developed to keep our species alive, they are truths of the human experience, and thereby hold objective weight in storytelling. 

I could say a lot more but my thoughts are too disjointed rn, but I can elaborate if you have any specific questions.
